title: Variety Is the Spice of Math Class
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane attributes his classroom's engagement not to strong classroom-management skills or standout test scores, but to running a deliberately varied 'toolbox' of activity types -- Do Now retrieval practice, daily puzzles, reasoning routines, curriculum activities, Desmos tasks, paper practice built on variation theory, mini-whiteboard practice, real-world lessons, spaced practice, reflections, group quizzes, and weekly mathematician presentations. He argues the key to making this variety work without becoming chaotic is embedding stable routines within each activity type, sticking with the same puzzle format or reasoning routine for several weeks so the format itself becomes automatic even as the content changes. Different students gravitate to different activity types, which Kane frames as evidence that variety, not any single 'best' method, gives more students a foothold into participating. He closes with three cautions: moving too fast risks leaving struggling and special-education students behind, not every teacher needs this many routines at once, and engagement is not the same as learning.
points: Kane's core claim: engagement in his classroom comes not from strong classroom management or standout results, but from deliberately varying activity types so different students find different footholds into participating.

His strategy for preventing chaos: build stable, well-practiced routines within each activity type, holding the same puzzle format or reasoning routine constant for 3-5 weeks so the format itself becomes automatic even as content changes.

He offers concrete evidence that different students respond to different activity types -- one student who refused Do Nows loved Desmos lessons, while another who disliked the core curriculum thrived on reasoning routines.

His three explicit cautions: moving too fast risks leaving struggling and special-education students behind, not every teacher should adopt this many routines at once, and engagement is only a means to the actual goal of learning.
quotes: I don't have any magical secret to engagement, but I think one big piece is that we do a lot of different types of thinking in a typical math class. That variety gives kids lots of ways to participate.

One risk of having lots of different things happening in class is that it starts to feel chaotic. If I'm always giving directions explaining some new thing kids end up confused and frustrated and not learning very much.

We stick with the same puzzle type on the Do Now every 4-5 weeks. We spend time on them the first few days as kids learn how they work. Then I often don't go over them at all as students become more independent.

For instance, I had one student who hated my Do Nows. He would refuse to take them, and rip up the paper if I gave him one. But he loved Desmos lessons, and would be excited to explore and share his ideas in that context.

Finally, I have to remember that engagement is not the same as learning... If my only goal is engagement I'll end up teaching a bunch of fun but poorly sequenced activities that keep kids busy and happy but don't teach very much.
